# Crown gall: a plant disease that became a tool

<!-- STEP id="disease" -->
## Swellings on the stem

Plant pathologists, scientists who study plant diseases, have seen a disease called crown gall disease. In this disease, tumour-like swellings develop on the stems because the cells there divide rapidly and without control. The disease is caused by a bacterium called *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*.

<!-- STEP id="study" -->
## How the bacterium passes in its genes

Instead of only trying to cure this disease, scientists studied how the bacterium transfers its genetic material into plant cells. This matters because a plant cell has a wall and a membrane, so genes cannot simply be poured in from outside. The bacterium passes its genetic material in, usually where the stem is wounded.

<!-- STEP id="tool" -->
## A tool for useful genes

This knowledge was later used in plant tissue culture and genetic engineering. Scientists can take out the bacterium's genes that cause the swelling and put a useful gene in their place. Today, *Agrobacterium* is used to introduce useful genes into plants for:

- the production of valuable phytochemicals, which are useful chemicals made by plants;
- improved crops;
- disease-resistant varieties.

<!-- STEP id="whole-plant" -->
## One changed cell, one whole plant

Because plant cells are totipotent, a single cell that has taken in the useful gene can be grown by tissue culture into a whole plant. Every cell of that plant then carries the new gene.

**By studying a plant disease, scientists found a way to give plants useful new genes.**
